mood.label: Telling you what we already knew

verdict: The audience universally points out that containers were never meant to be security boundaries, treating the video's premise as ancient tech wisdom.
tldr: Viewers are flooding the comments to collectively state that containers are for dependency management and portability, not security—effectively saying 'Docker bros just discovered VMs.' There is also overwhelming enthusiasm for more high-level architectural trend videos rather than granular CVE deep-dives.

clickbait.reason: The title questions container safety, but seasoned developers feel the answer has been obvious for a decade.

themes.title: Containers were never security boundaries
themes.summary: Viewers heavily emphasize that containers are for packaging and dependency isolation, not hard security sandboxing, comparing them to shipping containers.

evidence.text: I never saw it as a security boundry, rather a application isolation. Each application has its own dependencies, versions etc.
evidence.author: @JohnSmith-yz7uh

evidence.text: Wait, since when containers were a security boundary? AFAIK they were always a convenient way to ship software.
evidence.author: @TBC256

evidence.text: most of us graybeard Unix developers have always understood containers ("zones"/"jails") as places to isolate workloads to reduce _dependency_ issues, rather than to isolate them for security. the fact that they were always running on the same hardware, same kernel, meant that there was never a guaranteed isolation for _security_ purposes. once you start trusting systems to do things they were nev
evidence.author: @justLedbetter

evidence.text: Containers weren’t and aren’t meant to be used for security. They’re to standardize running a piece of software or collection of pieces of software. Similar to shipping containers, which are used to standardize shipping methodology and logistics for transporting goods.
evidence.author: @lespacecowboy

themes.title: Finding CVEs means fixing them
themes.summary: Many argue that the rising count of kernel vulnerabilities isn't a sign of worsening security, but rather finding and closing hidden attack vectors.

evidence.text: Some people are worrying over the increase in kernel vulnerabilities - I see it the other way around. Every found vulnerability is a closed attack vector. Just because these bugs were previously undetected, doesn't mean we were more safe - they were just waiting to be zero days. Finding and fixing vulnerabilities is good. The more the better.
